one_line: This video uses celebrity examples, social media comments, and academic research to argue that women's beauty choices are driven by self-expression and social influences rather than the male gaze.

hook.what_happens: Celebrity portraits of Doja Cat, Cardi B, and Rihanna appear alongside critical comments from men about their makeup and hair.
hook.why_it_works: It immediately addresses a relatable social debate using high-profile celebrities and real social media comments.

onscreen_text.text:
Scott_Vlog
Who is this actually for?
1d Reply

Josh_Beats
Less makeup looks better
1d Reply
Appealing to men isn't the goal
Bonell, S., Austen, E., & Griffiths, S. (2022). Australian women's motivations for, and experiences of, cosmetic surgery: a qualitative investigation. Body Image, 41, 128-139.
Question: "Why did you pursue cosmetic procedures?"
Who do women actually get cosmetic work done for?
Rodgers, R. F., Hewitt, R. C., & Lashway, K. (2016). Sociocultural pressures and engagement with cosmetic products and procedures in adult women. Body Image, 19, 101-107.
Multiple interconnected factors shape beauty decisions

transcript.text: One thing a lot of guys don't get is that this is literally most women's attitude when making decisions about their looks.
Look at beauty trends: bleached eyebrows, colourful hair, gradient lips, laminated brows, unconventional nail shapes.
This is stuff men literally do not notice or even actively like.
If you're even somewhat plugged into the beauty industry, you know it's obviously not for the male gaze.
Indeed, when Bonell and colleagues asked women why they pursue cosmetic procedures, they reported doing it to feel more confident and better align their appearance with their self-image.
So, who do women actually get cosmetic work done for? The best answer is likely, simply, 'themselves'.
But the full truth is a bit more complicated.
Research by Rodgers and colleagues suggest that beauty ideals are shaped by media, peers, and social norms.
So, personal preferences and social influences are somewhat deeply intertwined.
Do you want us to analyze your face? Click the link in bio. acos.com

narrative_arc: Establish the premise that women do not dress or style themselves for male approval.
Provide examples of trends that men dislike or ignore but women love.
Introduce academic research showing cosmetic procedures are done for self-confidence.
Complicate the 'for themselves' narrative by showing how media and peers shape those desires.
Conclude that beauty choices are a mix of personal identity and social norms, leading to a CTA.

cta.what: Encourages viewers to get a personalized facial analysis by visiting acos.com.

what_makes_it_work: Uses academic citations to back up sociological claims, elevating it above standard social media commentary.
Highly visual diagrams and 3D animations break down complex psychological concepts.
Leverages recognizable celebrity imagery to maintain high engagement throughout.
